prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize on B036 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case is the most complete on the shortlist. It runs from proglucagon processing and the identification of the biologically active GLP-1 peptides, through human incretin physiology and the mechanisms of action in islets, brain and gut, to therapies whose effects on glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes have been confirmed independently in large randomized trials. Nobody in round 1 raised a maturity question, and I do not see one. The chair asks whether the citation rewards the discovery or the creation of long-acting drugs. I think it should reward the discovery of what GLP-1 is, which form is active and what it does, and I would let the wording carry the therapeutic consequence without naming a product. That is the criterion that settles the third slot: Holst and Drucker already carry the physiology and the mechanisms, and Mojsov supplies the identity of the active peptide, which Knudsen's engineering depends on. A single part is also cleaner than splitting one coherent story, and no second part has come forward that I find stronger than leaving the prize whole.
statement.case_against: The weakness is attribution, and I do not think round 2 resolves it. Habener is outside the credited names and has a real claim to the early proglucagon and peptide work, so any trio under-represents the discovery. Mojsov's priority on the active peptide is described as contested by every member, and all of us, myself included, are working from recollection rather than from evidence checked against the supplied material. If the committee concludes that her contribution cannot be sustained, the Knudsen version becomes the better configuration, and I would support it on those grounds rather than leave the third slot to a name the committee cannot defend. The other cost is that a physiology prize leaves out the engineer most responsible for what patients receive. I accept that this is a prize-scope judgement, not a settled allocation.

responses.point: Linnarsson moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, but says the Knudsen version would be better if the committee values transformation of care as much as discovery, and asks whether the physiology could not have become a drug without the specific half-life engineering.
responses.response: I agree with your move and with your framing that excluding Knudsen is a prize-scope decision, whereas excluding a discoverer is a credit decision. On your question, the half-life engineering was clearly needed for once-daily and once-weekly dosing, and I would not minimise it. But the engineering depended on knowing which truncated peptide is active, that it is degraded rapidly, and that its action is glucose-dependent. That knowledge came from the physiology, and it would have directed any group toward the same target. I therefore do not think the engineering changes the nature of the discovery. I share your condition, though: if our discussion shows the active-peptide credit for Mojsov cannot be supported, I would join you in moving to Knudsen. I am not hiding that dependency by treating the trio as settled.

responses.point: Perlmann asks that the limitation from Habener's absence be recorded when the citation is worded, and that the citation stay about GLP-1 biology and its therapeutic use, not a specific drug.
responses.response: I agree on both points and would answer the chair's question about Habener the same way. The citation should say discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and its active forms. It should not claim priority for a single finding, which is a more defensible wording given that the early peptide work extends beyond the credited names. The Habener gap should also go into the deliberation record as a known limitation of the three-person rule, so the trio is not read as a verdict that his work was peripheral. I would apply the principle consistently. We accept foundational work outside the credited names here, and I do not think that alone is a reason to disqualify B026, B031 or B047, though it does count against them when we compare them with a cleaner pair such as B006.

responses.point: Sandberg says the absence of Habener is a real weakness and not just a caveat, and that if the peptide-identification credit cannot be assigned fairly, the Mojsov slot weakens and Knudsen should be revisited. He also ranks B006 above B031 because the credited pair is the pivotal one.
responses.response: I agree that the absence of Habener is more than a caveat, and I will not claim it is neutral. Where I come out differently is on the consequence. Credit for the early peptide work being spread across several people is a reason for careful citation wording, but it does not remove the contribution that Mojsov made, which was specifically the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form. I still think her slot is more defensible than Knudsen's under a discovery criterion, and I would revisit it only if someone shows from the evidence that the active-peptide claim fails. On B031 versus B006, your point on attribution persuades me. Feldmann and Maini are a clean pair for the clinical principle, but the TNF cloning and antibody engineering lie outside them, while Mori and Walter are the pivotal pair for the unfolded protein response. I have therefore moved B006 into my alternatives.

responses.point: The chair says B031 is strong but that the principle has since been partly absorbed into later cytokine therapies, and that he sees B006 as working best as an alternative or second part because its clinical impact is still developing.
responses.response: Your point about later cytokine therapies is fair, and I accept it as the main maturity question for B031. Anti-TNF established that blocking one cytokine can control a chronic inflammatory disease, and that principle is now so widely used that it can look like background. That cuts both ways, since it also marks how large the impact was. Even so, I agree with you that B031 does not displace B036. On whether a second part is needed, I do not see a candidate whose case is strong enough to justify one, and the three-person limit leaves no room anyway if Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are credited and the prize cannot be expanded. I agree that B006 is a conceptual fit and not a therapeutic one, and would use it only as an alternative if the GLP-1 allocation stalls. I would not choose it as a replacement for B036.

responses.point: El-Manira says that consistency requires the committee to settle the principle on discovery versus development before treating B026 differently from B036, and that credit contested among discoverers is not a reason to drop one of them.
responses.response: I agree with the consistency point and would apply the discovery criterion in the same way to every candidate. For B036 the discovery chain is inside the credited names. For B026 the earlier BCR-ABL and oncogene discoveries and the imatinib chemistry are outside the credited trio. That is why I regard B036 as a better fit and B026 as a stronger candidate than my first ranking implied, though still a development prize on the supplied credit. I also agree that disputed credit among discoverers should not by itself remove Mojsov. We differ slightly on Knudsen: I would not say the committee could never credit her, but only that it should do so if it deliberately changes the criterion to therapeutic transformation, which I have not been persuaded to do.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be supported from the supplied evidence. I am working from recollection, and if it cannot, I would move to the Knudsen configuration.
Whether the Habener gap is best handled in the citation wording, the deliberation record, or both.
Whether the committee will apply the discovery-versus-development criterion consistently across B036, B026, B031 and B047.
Whether TNF blockade (B031) is late recognition or has been absorbed into general practice so that it reads as background, which I cannot judge from the shortlist alone.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to any credited name on the shortlist. My field of autoimmunity and rheumatology is topically close to B031 (TNF blockade) and more loosely to B014. I have named B031 as an alternative, so I flag that proximity again. It is topical and not a personal tie, and my listed co-authors and my Bergen affiliation do not connect me to Feldmann or Maini. If B031 moves from an alternative to a serious option in the vote, I would disclose it again and the committee could decide whether it matters.
